title: BARMM has a new parliament, but the guns still remain
summary: The peace process in the Mindanao region remains unfinished, with thousands of MILF combatants and weapons still awaiting full decommissioning

items: Violence in the Bangsamoro region continues as rival factions of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and political clans clash, undermining the peace process following recent parliamentary elections.

The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) reported increased conflict incidents and deaths in October, driven by personal grudges, clan feuds, and competition over illicit economic activities.

The new Bangsamoro parliament faces significant challenges in promoting stability and governance, with calls for accountability in addressing ongoing violence and the decommissioning of MILF combatants.

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The guns did not go silent in the Bangsamoro region, where rival factions of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), feuding political clans, and competing illicit economic interests threaten to undermine a fragile peace just as a newly elected parliament took office.

The September 14 parliamentary elections brought some of these fault lines into the open, with deadly clashes between supporters of the rival Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor said.

The rivalry runs deep within the MILF. The BFP is led by former MILF military chief and now Bangsamoro Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua, while the UBJP is the Front’s official political party.
Armed clashes and mob violence involving supporters of the two parties erupted during and after election day. One riot in Barangay Bagua II, Cotabato City, left three people dead on September 14.

For ACLED, the violence was a warning about the fragility of the predominantly Muslim region’s fledgling institutions. The peace process remains unfinished, with thousands of MILF combatants and weapons still awaiting full decommissioning.

“Such factionalist violence has resurfaced the urgency of completing the decommissioning process meant to get the MILF to give up its full arsenal of weapons. Coupled with intermittent political violence from other sources, such an easy recourse to arms will continue to put the region on edge,” Tomas Buenaventura, ACLED Asia-Pacific analyst, noted in a report.

The watchdog said the rivalry between the BFP and UBJP, which is led by MILF chairman and former Bangsamoro interim chief minister Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, could subside as both camps adjust to parliamentary politics, making further armed confrontations unlikely for now. Both parties have signaled a common interest in the success of the Bangsamoro government and the peace process.

Yet the electoral rivalry is only one part of a more troubling security picture. Violence persisted across the region in October, fueled by disputes that extended beyond party politics and reached into the longstanding rivalries and illicit economies that have made peace difficult to secure.

The Critical Events Monitoring System (CEMS) of a peacebuilding monitor, Climate Conflict Action Asia (CCAA), recorded 79 conflict incidents and 47 deaths in October, compared with 74 incidents and 34 deaths in September.

The incidents included deadly clashes, ambushes and shootings across several towns. Many were driven by personal grudges, clan feuds and competition over illicit economic activities, including the illegal drug trade, gunrunning, and cigarette smuggling.
CCAA recorded 16 incidents involving personal grudges and clan feuding in October, mostly concentrated in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Sur.

In Sultan sa Barongis, Maguindanao del Sur, fighting that began on September 30 between members of an MILF base command and an armed group linked to criminal activities continued until a temporary ceasefire took effect in the third week of October. The clashes displaced around 1,100 households, killed one person, and wounded 10 others.
In neighboring Ampatuan town, a longstanding clan feud erupted into a firefight on October 15, displacing around 40 families.

Election-related tensions also spilled into clan violence. In Taraka, Lanao del Sur, a shooting was carried out on October 3, in retaliation for the killing of an individual by two UBJP supporters during the parliamentary elections, CCAA said.

Attacks on local officials also continued despite the postponement of the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections. Several shootings targeting village officials in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte were reportedly linked to political rivalries and preparations for the 2028 elections.

Violence also affected indigenous communities. CCAA reported that a Teduray leader who was a barangay councillor in Datu Hoffer Ampatuan was shot dead on October 17, followed a day later by the shooting of two other Teduray people in Datu Unsay.

The attacks came despite the formal recognition of the Teduray and Lambangian ancestral domain earlier in October. The watchdog said indigenous communities, particularly women and children, continued to face heightened vulnerabilities, including rising reports of gender-based violence.

Competition over illicit economic activities also fueled deadly confrontations. Four people were killed in an ambush in Datu Anggal Midtimbang on October 26 in an incident allegedly linked to the illegal gun trade.

In Cotabato City, two Coast Guard personnel were killed and another wounded in an October 22 ambush involving armed men reportedly linked to cigarette smuggling. Three more people were killed in a shooting the following day in Timako Hill, although CCAA said the incidents were unrelated.

Based on ACLED’s count, Maguindanao del Sur recorded the highest number of political violence incidents in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) from January 1 to October 30, with 47 incidents.
Maguindanao del Norte ranked second with 31 incidents, followed by Lanao del Sur with 21, the Special Geographic Area with 19, and Basilan with 11.

The watchdog also identified persistent threats from the Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters and Islamic State-inspired Dawlah Islamiyah groups, although their activities did not significantly disrupt the September elections.

CCAA warned that the withdrawal of additional security forces deployed for the elections had exposed the limits of temporary security measures, allowing longstanding rivalries and illicit economic activities to continue driving armed confrontations.

The election of Macacua as chief minister comes at a critical juncture for the region, with the new parliament facing the challenge of advancing autonomy and development amid a fragile security environment.
ACLED said the immediate tensions between the BFP and UBJP could give way to a period of détente, but the continued circulation of MILF weapons and unresolved factional divisions remain concerns.

CCAA said the new regional leadership and the MILF must be held accountable for addressing persistent violence, governance issues and the incomplete decommissioning of combatants if the Bangsamoro is to achieve lasting peace and inclusive governance. – Rappler.com
